title: Purpose of MTF Configuration File
content: The configuration file in YAML format is essential for the MTF framework because it assigns logical channels to physical channels, defining which hardware interface is used for data reception and transmission. This configuration is the central component that ties together the entire test system, enabling communication between ECUs (Electronic Control Units), the test bench hardware, and other connected components. The configuration file represents the complete setup including tracers, logical channels, physical adapters, and devices, connecting them into a cohesive working system.
summary: YAML configuration file that maps logical channels to physical hardware, enabling MTF framework to manage test system communication.

title: System Communication and Abstraction Benefits
content: The configuration ensures proper communication between ECUs, the test bench, and other connected components through well-defined logical abstraction layers. A key benefit of this architecture is abstraction: the same test cases can run on different setups by only updating physical channel information while keeping logical channels unchanged. This enables hardware-agnostic test development, allowing test engineers to focus on test logic rather than physical hardware details. When hardware needs to be replaced or upgraded, only the configuration file needs modification, not the test logic itself.
summary: MTF configuration enables test portability through hardware abstraction, allowing identical tests to run on different hardware setups.

title: Configuration File Structure - Sections Overview
content: The MTF configuration file consists of three main sections: Channels (mandatory), Mappings (mandatory), and FrameworkConfig (optional). The Channels section defines all logical channels representing virtual abstractions of physical hardware. The Mappings section connects these logical channels to actual physical hardware devices, allowing the framework to know which hardware resource to use. The FrameworkConfig section (optional) provides advanced configuration for tracers, connected ECUs, publisher behavior, Ethernet topology, and diagnostics. The order of sections in the YAML file does not affect interpretation but is kept consistent for clarity and ease of understanding. Each section plays a critical role in defining the complete test system behavior.
summary: MTF configuration has three sections: Channels (logical definitions), Mappings (hardware connections), and FrameworkConfig (advanced settings).

title: Channels Section - Purpose and Logical Channel Concept
content: The Channels section defines logical channels which will later be mapped to physical channels. A logical channel is a virtual abstraction of a physical hardware channel such as CAN, LIN, Ethernet, IO, or serial. This abstraction layer allows test engineers to think in terms of logical communication interfaces rather than specific hardware implementations. For example, a test case might reference 'can_primary_ch1' without needing to know whether this is connected to a Capture Module (CM) on IP 192.168.1.5 or a different hardware setup. Before defining channels, users must understand available hardware, but should only include channels relevant to the test case to maintain configuration clarity and system performance.
summary: Logical channels are virtual abstractions of physical hardware interfaces defined in the Channels section for test portability.

title: Channel Naming Rules and Best Practices
content: Channel names must follow specific naming conventions: they must be unique across the configuration, meaningful and descriptive, can include letters, numbers (not at the start), and underscores without spaces or special characters. Examples of good channel names include can_ch1, eth_main, lin_comms, or io_sensors - names that reflect both the protocol and purpose. Channel names must also be case-sensitive, so 'Can_CH1' and 'can_ch1' are different channels. When working with AUTOSAR PDUs or signals, channel names or aliases must match Communication Matrix names for proper signal routing. For Ethernet listening, MTF searches for specific patterns like ETH-SOMEIP-SPY or generic patterns like CHANNEL-SPY or CHANNEL-PORT to identify spy/listening channels.
summary: Channel names must be unique, meaningful, lowercase-preferred, and follow snake_case convention without spaces or special characters.

title: Channel Configuration Fields and Properties
content: Each channel must include mandatory fields: Id (unique, user-defined identifier) and Type (communication type: CAN, CANFD, LIN, FLEXRAY, ETHERNET, IO, SERIAL, PS, or BRIDGE). Optional fields enhance channel configuration: Protocol specifies version for complex hardware (CAN2.0, CANFD, LIN2.3); LoggingName defines a custom name for logging and tracing outputs; TracerName links the channel to a tracer for logging data; LoggingBusIndex is optional for IO tracing and defines specific logging index or uses fallback rules; Alias provides alternative names useful for reuse and database matching. All field names are case-sensitive - incorrect casing may cause parsing errors. YAML uses indentation with spaces (not tabs) to define hierarchy, and proper indentation is critical for correct parsing.
summary: Channels require Id and Type fields; optional fields include Protocol, TracerName, LoggingName, LoggingBusIndex, and Alias.

title: AUTOSAR PDU and Signal Integration
content: When working with AUTOSAR PDUs or signals, channel names or aliases must match Communication Matrix names for proper signal routing and identification. This ensures that the framework can correctly correlate signals defined in ARXML files with the logical channels in the configuration. The mapping between AUTOSAR database identifiers and MTF channel names is critical for automated signal processing and test data correlation. This requirement applies to all channel types that carry AUTOSAR-defined signals, including CAN, LIN, FlexRay, and Ethernet channels.
summary: Channel names/aliases must match AUTOSAR Communication Matrix names for proper AUTOSAR PDU and signal processing.
examples: Signal SPEED_INFO mapped to channel speed_ecu

title: Mappings Section - Purpose and Overview
content: The Mappings section is used to connect logical channels (defined in the Channels section) to physical hardware devices and interfaces. It allows the framework to know which hardware resource to use when a logical channel is referenced in test cases. This section transforms the framework from a hardware-agnostic logical model into a concrete hardware-specific configuration. Mappings enable reusable tests and flexible hardware configurations by providing a clear separation between logical test descriptions and physical hardware details. The Mappings section can include multiple device types, each with specific configuration requirements: CM (Capture Modules), BTS (IO boards), PCAP (network adapters), Power Supplies, Serial ports, Relay boards, and various specialized devices.
summary: Mappings section connects logical channels to physical hardware devices, enabling hardware-specific configuration separate from test logic.

title: Supported Device Types in Mappings Section
content: Mappings support multiple device types, each serving specific test functions: CM (Capture Module) records CAN, LIN, FlexRay, and Ethernet traffic; BTS-Revo simulates buttons, sensors, and actuators with voltage/current control; PCAP manages Ethernet adapters for network communication; PowerSupply configures Genesys, Manson, or Stamos power supplies; Serial defines COM port connections; RelayBoards controls electrical switches via CAN; HH_Electrical_load simulates load conditions; LF_Reader enables LF antenna configuration; WinpkFilter handles Ethernet packet filtering; TUN/TAP bridges virtual and physical Ethernet; TE_Analog maps analog channels; and Shelly Relay provides Ethernet-controlled switching. Each device type has specific configuration fields reflecting its hardware characteristics and operational modes.
summary: Mappings support diverse device types: CM, BTS, PCAP, PowerSupply, Serial, Relays, Electrical Load, LF Reader, Filters, and Analog.

title: Capture Module (CM) Mapping - Overview and Fields
content: Capture Modules (CM) are used to record communication data from CAN, LIN, FlexRay, and Ethernet channels. Logical channels are mapped to CM hardware channels using configuration fields: Id (last byte of CM IP address, e.g., 10 for 192.168.1.10); Type (CAN_Combo or LIN_Combo indicating interface type); Buses (list of logical channel names this CM handles); HWChannel (physical channel ID on the CM hardware); OperationMode defines channel behavior: Normal (Tx + Rx), Spy (listen only), TxOnly (send only), RxOnly (receive only). For FlexRay channels, additional fields are required: KeySlot (slot for sync/startup signals), NodeType (ColdStartLeading, ColdStartFollowing, etc. for cluster participation), and WakeUpCluster (support for wake-up signals). The CM device typically has multiple physical channels, and each must be properly configured to match the logical channel requirements.
summary: Capture Modules record multi-protocol traffic with configurable operation modes and require Id, Type, Buses, HWChannel, and FlexRay-specific fields.

title: BTS-REVO Mapping - Purpose and Configuration
content: BTS-REVO is a device used to simulate buttons, sensors, and actuators in hardware-in-the-loop testing. Logical channels are mapped to BTS-REVO physical IO channels to control and monitor voltage, current, and signal states during testing. The mapping structure uses the 'BTS-Revo' key, under which 'Boards' contains devices indexed by numbers. Each board has an Id (last byte of IP) and IOs list defining channel configurations. Important fields include: ChannelName (logical channel name), HWChannel (physical pin on the board), MeasurementAttribute (Voltage, Current, PWM), and Function (Relay, VBATSwitch, etc.). Optional fields include LineContactState, GndContactState, VbatContactState for contact state monitoring, StaticChannel for static configuration, InitValue for initialization, ChannelType, MeasurementConfig, and PWMWindowTime. BTS-REVO supports simulating fault conditions like short to ground, short to VBAT, and open load. The device has 24 IO channels, numbered starting from the connector farthest from power.
summary: BTS-REVO simulates IO signals and faults with channel-level voltage/current control via 24 IO pins mapped to logical channels.

title: Network Adapter (PCAP) Mapping - Configuration and Best Practices
content: Network adapters (PCAP) are used for Ethernet communication and packet capture. They can be physical or virtual and are mapped to logical channels for network traffic handling. PCAP mapping uses fields: Name (adapter name), FriendlyName (display name), Interface (network interface identifier), BufferSize, BpfFilter (Berkeley Packet Filter rules), Timeout (capture timeout), TimeStampPrecision, ImmediateMode, SnapshotLength, PacketProcessingActive, and PacketIdentificationActive. Advanced options include UseDataLoggerTimeStamp, RemoveDataLoggerMetaData, DataLoggerType, DifferentHandlerForTxAndRx, and TECMPPacketizationActive. Best practices: For logging-only scenarios, disable PacketProcessingActive and PacketIdentificationActive, increase Timeout, and disable ImmediateMode to reduce CPU overhead. For active bus listening, enable both processing and identification to ensure all traffic is properly handled. Adapter selection and configuration directly impact test performance and reliability.
summary: PCAP adapters enable Ethernet communication with configurable packet filtering, timestamping, and processing modes for network testing.
examples: Active listening adapter with packet identification

title: Power Supply Mapping - Genesys, Manson, and Stamos
content: Power supplies (Genesys, Manson, Stamos) can be mapped to logical channels, with each channel representing a power output with configurable voltage and current. Common fields include ChannelName (logical channel), DefaultVoltage, MaxVoltage, DefaultMaxCurrent, SamplingInterval, PortName (COM port for serial), ContinuousMonitoringActive, KeepStatus, and BitRate. Genesys supplies require additional fields: CommunicationProtocol (Serial or TCP), IP and Port (for TCP), Language (SCPI or GEN). Manson supplies typically use serial communication via COM ports with specific baud rates. The configuration allows precise control over power delivery parameters, enabling test scenarios that require specific voltage/current profiles.
summary: Power supplies map logical channels to physical power outputs with voltage/current control via serial or TCP communication.

title: Serial Mapping - Configuration and Protocol Settings
content: Serial mapping is used to connect logical channels to physical COM ports for serial communication between devices. Configuration fields include PortName (e.g., COM1, COM19), BaudRate, Parity (Even, Odd, None), DataBits, StopBits, FlowControl, MessageTerminator (defines end-of-line characters like CR, LF, or both for message boundary detection), SeparationTimeMs (time between messages), and MaxReceivedDataSize. MessageTerminator is particularly important as it defines how the framework detects message boundaries in serial data streams. Different protocols may use CR (Carriage Return), LF (Line Feed), or combinations thereof. Serial mapping is commonly used for device communication, logging interfaces, or specialized hardware that uses serial protocols.
summary: Serial mapping connects logical channels to COM ports with configurable baud rate, data format, and message terminator settings.

title: Relay Boards Mapping - CAN-Based Relay Control
content: Relay boards are used to control electrical switches via CAN channel communication. Relay mapping includes CANChannelName (logical channel), Boards (board list), Id (board identifier), Relays (relay configurations), HWChannel (physical relay index), InitValue (initialization state), DefaultValue (default state), and Function (relay behavior type). HID Relay Boards specifically use ID and Relays configuration with HWChannel and default states for each relay. Relay boards enable test scenarios requiring electrical switching such as power control, circuit isolation, or operational mode changes without direct ECU commands.
summary: Relay boards control electrical switches via CAN communication for voltage/circuit control in test environments.

title: HH Electrical Load Mapping - Load Simulation
content: HH Electrical Load is an external device used to simulate electrical load conditions in testing scenarios. It supports PLI (single channel) and PMLI (multi-channel) series devices. The mapping structure uses HH_Electrical_load key with Devices list. Each device configuration includes Id (device identifier), PortName (serial COM port), Type (PLI or PMLI), BitRate, and Channels mapping logical channel names to channel indexes. Main fields include PortName, BaudRate, ExternalTrigger, and VoltageProtection settings. HH Electrical Load enables realistic power consumption testing by simulating current draws on power supply outputs.
summary: HH Electrical Load simulates realistic power consumption conditions via serial communication with PLI or PMLI device types.

title: FrameworkConfig Section - Advanced Configuration Overview
content: The FrameworkConfig section is optional but used to configure advanced framework behavior such as tracers, connected ECUs, service packs, publisher settings, Ethernet configuration, diagnostics, Shelly relays, and optional channel fault injection settings. This section allows fine-tuning of the framework's runtime behavior beyond simple channel and device mapping. FrameworkConfig settings control how the framework processes data, routes traffic, synchronizes components, and handles communication at higher abstraction levels. All FrameworkConfig settings are optional, following the principle of default behavior with optional overrides.
summary: FrameworkConfig provides optional advanced settings for tracers, ECUs, networking, and framework behavior tuning.

title: Tracers - Data Logging Configuration
content: Tracers define how data is logged from different communication channels. Each tracer is named and configured separately and can be linked to multiple logical channels to record traffic such as CAN, Ethernet, or FlexRay. PCAP tracers are used for Ethernet packet capture with support for MultipleAdapterMode (logs multiple network adapters into single file) and PerformanceMode (high-speed optimized logging using buffers and burst writing). ASCII tracers log data in human-readable format supporting Hex or Decimal formatting, timestamp configuration (Absolute or Relative), and internal event logging. PCAP FileConfig defines file extension, compression (zstd), base file name, and file rotation settings. PCAP BufferConfig controls buffer size, number of buffers, and write burst size to avoid packet loss. ASCII tracer configuration includes Base formatting, InternalEventLogged flag, timestamp mode, and file configuration with BaseFileName, Extension, MaxFile, and MaxFileSize for rotation.
summary: Tracers enable flexible data logging via PCAP (Ethernet packets) or ASCII (human-readable) formats with performance optimization options.

title: Connected ECUs and Service Pack Configuration
content: ConnectedEcus defines the list of ECUs under test. Each ECU name must match identifiers in database files such as ARXML, DBC, LDF, or FIBEX files. This matching enables automatic signal processing and test data correlation. ServicePack groups multiple ECUs belonging to the same OEM and serves as an alternative to listing ECUs individually in ConnectedEcus. Using ServicePacks simplifies configuration for multi-ECU systems from the same manufacturer. The framework uses ECU definitions to resolve signal mappings, determine communication paths, and validate test case signals against configured ECUs.
summary: Connected ECUs and ServicePacks enable signal resolution and multi-ECU test configuration with database integration.

title: Publisher Configuration - Event Dispatching
content: PublisherConfig defines how events are dispatched in the framework using SingleThreaded or MultiThreaded modes. SingleThreaded mode processes all events sequentially in a single thread, suitable for simple test scenarios. MultiThreaded mode allows grouping channels into different processing threads, enabling parallel event processing for improved performance in complex multi-channel scenarios. This configuration directly impacts system performance, latency, and resource utilization. MultiThreaded configuration should be matched to available CPU cores and expected event volume.
summary: Publisher configuration controls event dispatching via SingleThreaded or MultiThreaded modes for performance tuning.

title: Ethernet Configuration - NPDU, SOME/IP, and Topology
content: Ethernet configuration consists of multiple components: NPduConfig manages VLAN tagging, IP-MAC mapping, and restrictions for Ethernet communication between ECUs, enabling controlled COM layer packet generation. SomeIPConfig defines server-to-client port mappings, endpoint implementation (boost or lwip), and adapter selection for Ethernet communication using SOME/IP protocol. AppLayerPorts defines port ranges for protocols such as NPdu, SomeIP, UDPNM, DLT, and SomeIpSD to control communication boundaries at application layer. EthernetTopology defines ECU-level network behavior including IP/MAC mapping, VLAN tagging, and protocol-based priority rules for Ethernet traffic handling. ChannelToEcusMapping links logical Ethernet channels to ECUs, allowing the framework to route Ethernet traffic through correct physical interfaces. Together, these settings enable sophisticated Ethernet test scenarios with realistic protocol behavior.
summary: Ethernet configuration manages VLAN tagging, IP-MAC mapping, SOME/IP protocol, and ECU routing for complex network testing.

title: Diagnostics Configuration - ECU Diagnostic Sessions
content: Diagnostics section configures ECU diagnostic sessions for testing diagnostic functionality. Configuration includes protocol selection (DOIP - Diagnostics over IP or HSFZ), ECU IP address, tester IP (test equipment IP), and optional network ID filtering. The framework uses these settings to establish proper diagnostic communication channels with ECUs in the test environment. Proper diagnostics configuration is essential for functional safety testing and system validation.
summary: Diagnostics configuration enables ECU diagnostic session testing via DOIP or HSFZ protocols with IP routing.

title: Fault Injection - ChannelsConfig for Network Faults
content: ChannelsConfig defines faulty channels used for injecting hardware faults such as short circuit or open wire conditions on CAN, LIN, or IO channels for testing robustness. Fault injection allows testing ECU behavior under adverse conditions without actual hardware failures. This capability is critical for validating error handling, robustness, and safety mechanisms in embedded systems. Fault types simulate realistic failure modes that could occur in field conditions.
summary: Fault injection via ChannelsConfig simulates network and hardware failures to test ECU robustness and error handling.

title: Time Synchronization (EES) - GrandMaster Configuration
content: EES (Ethernet Equipment Synchronization) provides nanosecond-level synchronization for test bench devices using a GrandMaster configuration. The GrandMaster field defines which EES device is responsible for time synchronization in the system. Precise time synchronization is critical for multi-device testing scenarios where timing correlation between devices is essential for test validity. This is particularly important for FlexRay testing and complex multi-protocol scenarios.
summary: EES provides nanosecond-level time synchronization across test devices via GrandMaster configuration.

title: Special Devices - TE Analog, WinpkFilter, TUN/TAP, Shelly Relay
content: TE-Analog maps analog channels from devices like LIN and CM-sense to logical channels using fields ChannelName, HWChannel, and DeviceId. WinpkFilter is used for Ethernet packet filtering and manipulation using adapters and IP/MAC/VLAN rules with fields AdapterFriendlyName, Type (Filter or FilterFastIO), IPMacTable, and VLAN configuration. TUN/TAP bridges virtual adapters with physical Ethernet adapters allowing VLAN tagging and packet manipulation, including ETH_Bridge, PhysicalAdapter, TunTapAdapterList, InnerVlan, and OuterVlan configuration. Shelly Relay is an Ethernet-controlled relay supporting HTTP/MQTT with fields IP, Port, CommunicationProtocol, Channels, DoRestart, RestartDuration, and DurationAfterRestart. These specialized devices enable advanced testing scenarios beyond standard channel communication.
summary: Special devices enable analog mapping, packet filtering, virtual bridging, and Ethernet relay control for advanced test scenarios.

title: System Performance Notes - Network Protection and Optimization
content: Network protection or antivirus services should be disabled in test environments to avoid performance degradation when using hardware modules like CM, BTS, or EES systems. Real-time communication requirements of test hardware necessitate minimal OS interference. PCap-based Ethernet testing particularly benefits from disabled network filtering to achieve consistent capture timing and avoid packet loss. For optimal performance: disable Windows Defender in test environments; disable third-party firewalls during testing; configure CPU affinity for critical test threads; use dedicated network interfaces for test traffic when possible; monitor CPU utilization and adjust MultiThreaded publisher settings accordingly.
summary: Disable network protection/antivirus in test environments to maintain performance with hardware modules and real-time requirements.
